column2: So too the aged son of Shantanu (Bhishma), the Brahmana Bahlika, Drona, Somadatta and Bhurishravas—
Amitaujas, Yudhamanyu and the valiant Uttamaujas, having slain hundreds of heroes, were themselves slain in battle by the enemy.
Kshatradharman the Panchala and Kshatravarman, O revered one, both mighty archers, were sent to Yama's abode by Drona.
Kshatradeva, son of Shikhandin and lord of warriors, was slain in battle by Lakshmana, your grandson, O Bharata.
Suchitra and Chitradharman, father and son, great chariot-warriors of great valour, moving in battle, were slain by Drona.
Vriddhakshemi, O great king, having wrought slaughter in battle, was felled by the Kaurava Bahlika.
Dhrishtaketu, O great king, foremost chariot-warrior of the Chedis, having done a deed not easy to do, went to Yama's abode.
So too Satyadhriti, dear one, having wrought slaughter in battle and fought valiantly for the Pandavas, was sent to Yama's abode.
Sukétu, son of Shishupala, O lord of the earth, having slain foes in battle, was himself slain in battle by Drona.
Likewise the hero Satyadhriti, the valiant Madirashva and the brave Suryadatta were slain by Drona's arrows.
Shrenimat too, O great king, fighting valiantly, having done a deed not easy to do, went to Yama's abode.
So also the valiant king of Magadha, slayer of heroes, fighting bravely, was slain by Bhishma, O king.
Vasudana, wreaking great slaughter in the fight, was sent to Yama's abode by Bharadvaja's son through his prowess.
These and many other great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas were slain by Drona's prowess—this is what you ask me.
[Dhritarashtra said:] O best of speakers, in this army of mine whose heroes are slain, tell me, charioteer, who here are alive and unslain.
Those you have named are slain today; those whom you consider unslain I also count as already won heaven.
[Sanjaya said:] Into whom, O king, the great weapons—wondrous, bright, of four kinds, divine—were placed by Drona, the hero, best of the twice-born,
that great chariot-warrior, skilled, quick-handed, of firm weapons, firm fist and firm arrows, the valiant and energetic son of Drona, stands ready to fight for your sake.
The dweller in Anarta, son of Hridika (Kritavarman), great chariot-warrior, foremost of the Satvatas, Bhoja himself, skilled in weapons, stands ready to fight for your sake.
Sharadvata Gautama (Kripa) too, O king, of great strength, a warrior of many wondrous weapons, grasping his great and wondrous bow able to bear a burden, stands ready to fight.
Artayani (Shalya), unshakable in battle, the first leader of your army, letting go those Pandavas dearer to him than his own, wishes to make his word true.
Shalya, who had promised before Ajatashatru to blunt the splendour of the charioteer's son in battle, unassailable and equal to Shakra in prowess, stands ready to fight for your sake.
With horses of noble breed, Sindhus, mountaineers, men from the rivers, Kambojas, forest-dwellers and Bahlikas, the king of Gandhara with his own force stands ready to fight for your sake.
So too your son, mounting a chariot blazing like the sun, O hero of the Kurus, stands ready, friend of the Kurus, O lord of men, like the shining sun in a cloudless sky.
Duryodhana, of great valour, amid the line of elephants and the best of warriors, on a chariot adorned with gold, stands ready in battle, eager to fight.
That foremost of men in the midst of kings shone, in variegated golden armour, like a fire with little smoke, lotus-hued, like the sun amid clouds.
Likewise Sushena, sword and shield in hand, your son, and the hero Satyasena, together with Chitrasena, joyful in spirit, stand ready to fight.
Hrinishedha, the Bharatas, the princes, Chitrayudha, Shrutakarman, Jaya, Shala, Satyavrata and Dushala, the mighty, stand ready, eager to fight.
The lord of the Kaitavyas, proud of his heroism, a prince who slays foes in battle after battle, going forth with infantry, horses and elephant-chariots, stands ready to fight for your sake.
The hero Shrutayus and Shrutayudha, Chitrangada and the hero Chitravarman, and the foremost men of the army who stand ready—strikers, proud and true to their word.

Karna's great-souled son Satyasena stands ready, eager to fight, and two other worthy sons of Karna, quick-handed, O lord of men, standing in the great host hard to break by the faint-hearted, are ready to fight for your sake.
With these chief warriors and others, O king, heroes of immeasurable power, the king of the Kurus stands amid the line of elephants like Mahendra, intent on victory.
[Dhritarashtra said:] You have told me truly of those still alive among the enemy; thus I plainly understand the matter from what has been obtained.

[Vaishampayana said:] As he was speaking thus, Dhritarashtra, Ambika's son, hearing of his army with its heroes slain, shattered and with little left, fell into bewilderment, his senses overwhelmed with grief.
Faint, he said, "Wait a moment, Sanjaya; my mind is disturbed, dear one, having heard so very unwelcome a thing." Then that lord of the earth lost consciousness.
He met with the greatest sorrow, born of calamity to his sons. Tell me, who ask, what he said at that time.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing of Karna's death, wondrous and almost beyond belief, confounding all beings, dreadful like the toppling of Mount Meru,
like the improper bewilderment of the mind of the great-minded Bhargava, like the defeat of Indra of dreadful deeds at the hands of his foes,
like the sun of great splendour falling from heaven to earth, like the unimaginable drying up of the ocean of inexhaustible waters,
like the wondrous total destruction of earth, sky and the quarters, like the fruitlessness of both deeds, meritorious and sinful,
Dhritarashtra, lord of men, reflecting skilfully with his understanding, thinking of Karna's death, "This cannot be,"
yet, since it is the nature of beings, it may be so—such was his thought of destruction; his mind, burning with the fire of grief, was as if blown upon by a bellows.
With ruined spirit, sighing, dejected, exclaiming "Alas!", deeply afflicted, Dhritarashtra, Ambika's son, lamented, O great king.

He who like a bull never turned back from battle even against a bull, a youth of body hard as the thunderbolt even to Mahendra's foe,
mahabharata:8:5.12	at the twang of whose bowstring and the sound of whose rain of arrows chariots, horses, men and elephants could not stand in battle,
mahabharata:8:5.13	relying on whom, the mighty-armed slayer of the hosts of enemies, the unfallen, Duryodhana made enmity with the mighty sons of Pandu—
mahabharata:8:5.14	how was that Karna, best of chariot-warriors, tiger among men, of irresistible and invincible prowess, slain in battle by Partha?
mahabharata:8:5.15	He who, relying on the strength of his own arms, never regarded Achyuta (Krishna) nor Dhananjaya nor the Vrishnis nor others,
mahabharata:8:5.16	saying, 'I alone, from my divine chariot, will fell in battle the two unconquered bowmen, the wielders of Sharnga and Gandiva, together,'
mahabharata:8:5.17	so he always said to Duryodhana, who was foolish, greed-deluded, not poor, longing for the kingdom, and over-eager;
mahabharata:8:5.18	he who conquered the exceedingly strong and hard-to-conquer foes—the Gandharas, Madrakas, Matsyas, Trigartas, Tanganas and Shakas,
mahabharata:8:5.19	the Panchalas, Videhas, Kunindas, Kashi-Kosalas, Suhmas, Angas, Pundras, Nishadas, Vangas and Kichakas,
mahabharata:8:5.20	the Vatsas, Kalingas, Taralas, Ashmakas and Rishikas, and who, a hero having conquered them in battle, made them tribute-payers of old.
mahabharata:8:5.21	Among horses Uchchaihshravas is best, among kings Vaishravana, among gods Mahendra; among strikers Karna was best—
mahabharata:8:5.22	obtaining whom, the king of Magadha, with conciliation and honours, besieged the kshatriyas of the earth except the Kauravas and Yadavas.
mahabharata:8:5.23	Hearing that Karna was slain in single combat by Savyasachin, I am sunk in an ocean of grief, like one without a raft in the sea.
mahabharata:8:5.24	If I do not perish, Sanjaya, from such sorrows, I deem my heart harder than the thunderbolt and hard to break.
mahabharata:8:5.25	What other man in the world but myself, hearing of this defeat of kinsmen, relatives and friends, would not cast off life, charioteer?
mahabharata:8:5.26	I would choose poison, fire, or a leap from a mountain peak; I cannot bear these painful sorrows, Sanjaya.
[Sanjaya said:] "In fortune, family, fame, austerity and learning, the good today regard you as Yayati, son of Nahusha.
In learning you are like a great sage, you have done what is to be done, O king; compose yourself, do not yield to despair."
[Dhritarashtra said:] "I deem fate alone supreme; fie on human effort, which is useless, where Karna, like Rama, was slain in battle.
Having slain Yudhishthira's army and throngs of Panchala chariots, scorching all quarters with showers of arrows, the great chariot-warrior,
having bewildered the Parthas in battle as the thunderbolt-wielder confounds asuras, how does he lie slain, like a tree broken by the wind?
I see no end to my grief, like the waves of the ocean; fierce anxiety grows in me and a longing to die arises.
Hearing of Karna's death and Phalguna's victory, I deem Karna's slaying beyond belief, Sanjaya.
Surely my heart is made of thunderbolt-essence and very firm, since it does not burst on hearing that Karna, tiger among men, is slain.
Surely a very long life was ordained for me by the gods of old, since hearing that Karna is slain I live here in deepest sorrow.
Fie on this life of mine, Sanjaya, bereft of friends. Reduced today to this despised state, I shall live wretchedly, pitiable to all, dull-witted.
I who was once honoured by all the world, how shall I, charioteer, bear to live, humbled? I have fallen into a calamity worse than sorrow, Sanjaya.
Therefore, with the slaying of Bhishma and of the great-souled Drona, and now with the charioteer's son slain in battle, I see nothing remaining here.
He was the far shore for my sons, Sanjaya; that hero was slain in battle, though he let fly many arrows.
What use is life to me without that bull among men? Surely that atiratha, tormented by arrows, fell from his chariot,
like a mountain peak split by a thunderbolt. Surely he lies adorning the earth, drenched in blood, like an elephant felled by a rutting elephant.
The strength of Dhritarashtra's sons, from whom the Pandavas feared, that Karna, peer of bowmen, was slain by Arjuna.
That hero, mighty archer, who gave my sons fearlessness, lies slain, like Bala slain by Shakra.
Like a lame man's journey, a pauper's desire, a thirsty man's hope of water, so was Duryodhana's intention.
What is planned one way comes out another way. Ah, fate is mighty and time is hard to overcome!
Fleeing wretchedly, dejected, his manhood lost—I hope my son Duhshasana, the charioteer's son's friend, was not slain.
I hope, dear one, he did nothing base in battle; I hope that hero was not slain in such a way that kshatriyas should not have been slain.
Yudhishthira always said, 'Let there be no war', but Duryodhana, foolish, did not accept it, as one does not accept wholesome medicine.
Bhishma, the great-souled, lying on his bed of arrows, asked Partha for water, and Partha pierced the surface of the earth.
Seeing the stream of water produced by the Pandava, that mighty-armed one said, 'My dear, make peace with the Pandavas.
From calm may come peace, and let the war end with my death; enjoy the earth with the sons of Pandu in brotherhood.'
Not following his words, my son surely grieves now; the word of the far-sighted one has come true.
But I, Sanjaya, with my ministers slain and my sons slain, fallen into distress through the dice, am like a bird with clipped wings.
As boys in play seize a bird, clip its wings and joyfully release it, Sanjaya,
with its wings clipped it cannot fly away; so I too have become like a bird with clipped wings.
Wasted, bereft of all that matters, without kin, cut off from relatives, which way shall I go, dejected and fallen under the power of my foes?
He who conquered the earth for the increase of Duryodhana, the lord, has been conquered by the valiant, capable and mighty Pandavas.
When that mighty archer Karna was slain in battle by Kiritin, which heroes turned back? Tell me that, Sanjaya.
I hope no single man was left abandoned and slain in battle by the Pandavas. Tell me, hero, how the heroes were felled, as you told it before.
Bhishma, who did not fight back, Shikhandin felled in battle with the best of arrows—the best of all weapon-bearers.
So too Drona, having laid down all weapons in battle, in yogic meditation, the mighty archer, pierced by many arrows, was slain by Dhrishtadyumna with raised sword, Sanjaya.
These two were killed through intermediary means and especially by deceit; I heard that Bhishma and Drona were felled.
In battle the thunderbolt-wielder himself could not slay Bhishma and Drona if they fought fairly; this I tell you as truth.
But how did death touch Karna, a hero like Indra, who hurled divine weapons in great number?
Karna, to whom Purandara (Indra) gave, in exchange for his earrings, the divine dart bright as lightning, adorned with gold, slayer of foes,
whose divine arrow with serpent's mouth, adorned with gold, lay among the sandalwood, a slayer of enemies,
who despised the great chariot-warriors led by Bhishma and Drona and learned the dreadful Brahma weapon from Jamadagni's son,
who, seeing those led by Drona turned away and tormented by arrows, shattered the bow of Subhadra's son with arrows,
who, having left Bhimasena, brother of ten thousand elephants' strength and wind-swift speed, without a chariot, laughed at him,
who, having defeated Sahadeva with arrows of straight joints, left him chariotless out of pity, and did not kill him, knowing dharma,
who destroyed thousands of illusions, and having overcome the fierce Ghatotkacha, lord of rakshasas, struck him down with Shakra's dart—
for all these days Dhananjaya, fearing him, did not come to single combat; how was that hero slain in battle?
If his chariot was not stuck, nor his bow shattered, nor his weapons lost, how was he slain by the enemy?
Who in battle is able to conquer Karna, tiger among men, swift as a tiger, brandishing his great bow, loosing dreadful arrows and divine weapons?
Surely his bow was cut or his chariot sank into the earth or his weapons vanished, as you say he is slain; for I see no other cause of his destruction.
'Until I slay Arjuna I will not wash my feet'—such was the dreadful vow of that great soul,
fearing whom Yudhishthira, king of dharma, best of men, did not sleep for thirteen years in the forest.
Relying on the strength of that mighty great soul, my son forcibly took the wife of the Pandavas to the assembly.
And there too, in the midst of the assembly, in the sight of the Pandavas, he called Panchali a slave-woman in the Kuru court.
He who, not heeding the fierce touch of arrows shot from Gandiva, said, 'You have no husband, Krishna,' and glanced at the Parthas,
he who felt no fear of the Parthas with their sons and with Janardana, relying on the strength of his own arms, even for a moment, Sanjaya—
I do not think he could be slain even by the gods with Vasava, as they rushed against him; how much less by the Pandavas, dear one?
For when he touched the bowstring and took hold of the guard, no man could stand before the son of Adhiratha.
The earth might be without the light of moon and sun, but not the slaying of that lord of men who never fled in battles.
If that fool, with his helper and brother Duhshasana, ill-advised, chose to refuse Vasudeva's proposal,
surely, seeing Karna, with shoulders like a bull's, felled, and Duhshasana slain, my son grieves.
Hearing that Vaikartana was slain in single combat by Savyasachin, and seeing the Pandavas victorious, what did Duryodhana say?
Hearing that Durmarshana and Vrishasena had been slain in battle, and seeing his army broken and being struck down by great chariot-warriors,
and seeing the kings turned away, intent on flight, the chariot-warriors routed, I think my son grieves.
Inexorable in pride, childish in understanding, impatient—seeing his army's spirit broken, what did Duryodhana say?
Seeing his brother slain in battle by Bhimasena who was drinking his blood, what did Duryodhana say?
What did Karna, who had spoken in the assembly together with the king of Gandhara that he would slay Arjuna in battle, say when Arjuna was not slain?
Shakuni, son of Subala, who in the past, having played at dice, rejoiced and cheated the Pandavas, what did he say, dear one, when Karna was slain?
Kritavarman, the mighty archer, great chariot-warrior of the Satvatas, son of Hridika, seeing Karna slain, what did he say?
He whose instruction Brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas, desiring the science of the bow, attend—the wise son of Drona—
Ashvatthaman, young, handsome, of great renown, what did he say, Sanjaya, when Karna was slain?
Kripa Sharadvata, who attained the rank of teacher in archery and knows the highest truth, what did he say, dear one, when Karna was slain?
Shalya, king of the Madras, mighty archer, ornament of assemblies—surely all of that was fated, how Karna was felled.
And whatever kings had come to the earth to fight, what did they say, Sanjaya, on seeing Vaikartana slain?
When Karna, hero, tiger among chariot-warriors, bull among men, was slain, what was the front of your divisions like, Sanjaya, section by section?
How was Shalya, king of the Madras, best of chariot-warriors, appointed as Vaikartana's charioteer? Tell me that, Sanjaya.
Who guarded the right wheel of the charioteer's son in battle, who guarded the left wheel, and who was behind the hero?
Which heroes deserted Karna, which cowards ran away in fear, and how was the great chariot-warrior Karna slain while all of you were together?
And how did the Pandava heroes confront that great chariot-warrior as he poured down showers of arrows like a cloud pouring streams of water?
And how did that divine, serpent-mouthed, foremost of great arrows become useless then? Tell me that, Sanjaya.
I see no remnant of my army, Sanjaya, whose pride is gone, now that its hump has been crushed.
Hearing that those two heroes, mighty archers, best of the Kurus, Bhishma and Drona, were slain for my sake, what use is life to me?
I cannot bear that Radheya, the ornament of battle, is slain, whose arms' strength equalled hundreds upon hundreds of elephants.
Tell me, Sanjaya, what happened to the Kauravas, those heroes among men, in the war with the enemy after Drona was slain.
And tell how Karna joined battle with the sons of Kunti, and how the slayer of his foes was stilled in battle."
While the Kaurava army was fleeing, O great king, Partha arranged his own army and stood with his brothers.
Knowing him to be so placed and seeing his own army fleeing, your son, O best of the Bharatas, checked it by his manliness.
Having rallied his troops and relying on the strength of his arms, O Bharata, he fought a very long time with the Pandavas.
When the enemy, having attained their aims, joyful, and exerting themselves long, had been fought, at the approach of evening he ordered the retreat.
Having withdrawn the troops and entered his own camp, the Kurus then took counsel for their own good.
They sat on costly couches spread with rich coverlets, on excellent seats, like immortals reclining on comfortable beds.
Then King Duryodhana, addressing those mighty archers in very gentle and conciliatory words, spoke what the time required.
O best of the wise, all of you tell your minds without delay: in such a case, kings, what should be done that will be effective?

Attachment, application, skill and policy are the means of accomplishing a purpose, as the wise say; all of these depend on fate.
mahabharata:8:6.13	Those heroes of ours, world-famed, godlike great chariot-warriors, prudent, disciplined, skilful and devoted, have been slain.
mahabharata:8:6.14	Yet we should not despair of victory; when all measures are well taken here, even fate is made favourable.
mahabharata:8:6.15	So we, having made Karna, the foremost of men, endowed with every excellence, our commander, will crush our enemies.
Then Duryodhana, pleased on hearing those pleasant words, which were kindly, true, beneficial to himself and auspicious,
steadying his mind and relying on the strength of his arms, O great king, spoke to Radheya.

Karna, I know your valour and your supreme friendship to me; still, O mighty-armed, I shall speak to you words for your good.
mahabharata:8:6.19	Having heard, do as you please, hero of the Kurus, as it pleases you; you are the wisest of all and always my highest refuge.
mahabharata:8:6.20	The two atirathas Bhishma and Drona, my commanders, are slain; let you be commander, richer in merit than they.
mahabharata:8:6.21	Those two mighty archers were partial to Dhananjaya, yet I honoured them, Radheya, at your word.
mahabharata:8:6.22	Looking to Bhishma's seniority as grandsire, he protected the sons of Pandu in the great war, dear one, for only ten days.
mahabharata:8:6.23	And when Bhishma, our grandsire, laid down his weapons, he was slain by Phalguna in the great battle, putting Shikhandin before him.
mahabharata:8:6.24	When that illustrious one had fallen on the bed of arrows, then, at your word, tiger among men, Drona became our leader.
mahabharata:8:6.25	He too protected the Parthas in this battle because they were his pupils; and that aged one was swiftly slain by Dhrishtadyumna.
mahabharata:8:6.26	With those two chiefs slain, O one of immeasurable prowess, reflecting, I see no one but you equal to fighting in battle.
mahabharata:8:6.27	You alone are able to win us victory, without doubt; at the beginning, in the middle and at the end, that is known to you alone.
mahabharata:8:6.28	Therefore, like a draught-ox, you ought to bear the yoke in battle; consecrate yourself as commander.
mahabharata:8:6.29	As Skanda, the imperishable lord, is leader of the gods' army, so may you bear this army of Dhritarashtra's sons for me; slay all the hosts of foes as Mahendra the danavas.
mahabharata:8:6.30	Knowing you, the great chariot-warrior, to be firm in battle, the Pandavas with the Panchalas will flee as danavas on seeing Vishnu. Therefore, tiger among men, lead the great army.
I wish to hear this; tell it, best of the twice-born, for I am never satisfied with hearing the great deeds of my forefathers.
They stayed not far from the army camp, having turned back, wounded and bleeding on all sides by sharp weapons.
I have heard of Ashvatthaman's deed and of the curses laid on one another; tell the sequel, what Sanjaya said.
The great-souled siddhas and best of Brahmana sages came to the righteous king Yudhishthira, who had offered the water oblation.
Seeing my body covered with arrows and deep wounds, I find no peace, brooding on my evil deeds alone, hero.
As he sank down, Bhima, urged by Krishna, seized him, and Krishna, crusher of hostile hosts, said to him, "Not so."
For how long did my ancestors, the great-souled ones, remain in the kingdom? You ought to explain that to me.
Dreadful haloes were seen around the moon and sun, three-hued, dark, rough at the edges, and ash-red in lustre.
Time cooks all beings, O wise one; I regard renunciation of action as best. You too should see this.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hear what your forefathers, led by Yudhishthira, did after attaining heaven, the third realm.
